# 2 Kings 1 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Introduction and Background

The division of the Book of Kings at this point is arbitrary and artificial. The original Hebrew canon had Kings as a single book; the division comes from the Septuagint and Vulgate. The narrative of 2 Kings 1 continues directly from 1 Kings 22:51–53, breaking in the middle of Ahaziah's reign. This is noted by both Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary as "most unhappy" (Pulpit Commentary).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/1.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

---

## v. 1: *"After the death of Ahab, Moab rebelled against Israel."*

Moab had been subjected by David (2 Samuel 8:2) and, after the division of the kingdom, fell under the northern kingdom's control. Omri reconquered Moab, and Ahab maintained the suzerainty, extracting a heavy tribute (2 Kings 3:4 — 100,000 lambs and 100,000 rams with their wool). The "Moabite Stone" (discovered 1869) confirms Moab's subjection "forty years" under Omri and Ahab, and records King Mesha's rebellion. The death of Ahab in battle and Israel's defeat at Ramoth-gilead gave Mesha the opportunity to revolt. The Hebrew conjunction is the simple copulative ("and Moab rebelled"), implying sequence but also consequence — the weakening of Israel after Ahab's death emboldened subject peoples.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/1-1.htm (Pulpit and Gill)
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-1-commentary

David Guzik notes that while Ahab's reign was a spiritual disaster, it was also a time of political security and economic prosperity; his death therefore triggered instability.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/

The JFB Commentary notes that the rebellion was "accomplished as a providential judgment on the house of Ahab for all their crimes," and Ahaziah's accident prevented him from taking active measures to suppress it.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-kings-1.html (search result excerpt)

---

## v. 2: *"Now Ahaziah had fallen through the lattice of his upper room in Samaria and injured himself. So he sent messengers and instructed them: 'Go inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will recover from this injury.'"*

**The fall:** The "lattice" (Hebrew *sebakah*, from *sabak*, "to entwine") was a net-like wooden trellis or grid used to provide shade and air circulation on upper stories. Ahaziah apparently leaned against it or stepped where it was weak and fell through. This same word describes the net ornamentation on Solomon's temple pillars (1 Kings 7:17). Precept Austin notes the irony: Ahaziah's "accident" would be woven into God's bigger story — a battle between Yahweh and Baal, "Mount Carmel, Part 2."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-1-commentary
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

**Baal-zebub:** The name means "lord of flies" — either a god who sent flies as a plague, or one who averted them from his worshippers (analogous to the Greek *Zeus Apomyios* or Roman *Jupiter Myiagrus*). Flies were a terrible plague in the East. Ekron was the northernmost of the five chief Philistine cities, and the nearest Philistine shrine to Samaria. The Pulpit Commentary explains that Ahaziah, as a worshipper of Baal, "would naturally inquire of some form of the Baal divinity." Why Ekron specifically is unclear, but the Baal religious center at Ekron had a reputation for divination and soothsaying.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-1-commentary

**Ahaziah's idolatry:** Guzik calls Ahaziah a "practical atheist" — he believed Yahweh existed but lived as though He didn't. The king did not ask for healing, only for a prognostication. His messengers' journey was about 60 miles (three days one way). Ahaziah knew of Elijah's victory over Baal's prophets at Carmel and Micaiah's prophecy of his father's death, yet still turned to a pagan deity.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-1-commentary

Dr. Constable notes that Ahaziah may have sent to Ekron (rather than a local Baal shrine) to keep his illness a secret from political enemies.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-1.html (search result excerpt)

H.A. Ironside comments: "Men love the gods that are most like unto themselves, so it is not surprising to see Ahaziah sending to this miserable Philistine god."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/2-kings-1.html (search result excerpt)

---

## v. 3: *"But the angel of the LORD said to Elijah the Tishbite, 'Go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria and ask them, "Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are on your way to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?"'"*

**"The angel of the LORD":** The Pulpit Commentary translates it as "an angel" (following the LXX which has ἄγγελος without the article), noting an angel had appeared to Elijah before (1 Kings 19:5, 7). Dr. Constable, by contrast, sees this as perhaps "the preincarnate Christ," citing Genesis 16:9 and 1 Kings 19:7.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-1.html (search result excerpt)

**The rhetorical question:** The double negative ("Is it because there is no God…") is intensitive — it implies a "complete and absolute denial of the Divinity of Jehovah. To consult a foreign oracle is equivalent to saying that the voice of God is wholly silent in one's own land." This was going further in apostasy than Ahab had gone (Ahab at least consulted prophets of Yahweh on occasion, 1 Kings 22:6–9).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

Guzik emphasizes that Ahaziah believed Yahweh existed but "lived as if there were no God in Israel" — he was a "practical atheist."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/

---

## v. 4: *"Therefore this is what the LORD says: 'You will not get up from the bed on which you are lying. You will surely die.' So Elijah departed."*

The Hebrew *laken* ("therefore") is emphatic: "for this reason." Because Ahaziah had apostatized from God by consulting Baal-zebub, God sentenced him to die from the effects of his fall. The Pulpit Commentary notes it is "implied that he might have recovered if he had acted otherwise."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

Guzik interprets this as a mercy: "God told him something that few people know. His death was imminent, and he had time to repent and prepare to meet God." He also notes (citing Wiseman) that the phrasing "you will surely die" was styled like a medical prognosis — it was as if Elijah said, "Here's your diagnosis: Your condition is fatal and irreversible."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/

Gill notes simply: Elijah "departed" — he had said all he was commissioned to say and left the messengers.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/1.htm

---

## v. 5: *"When the messengers returned to the king, he asked them, 'Why have you returned?'"*

Ahaziah perceived they could not have gone to Ekron and back in the time elapsed, so he knew they had been intercepted. The Pulpit Commentary renders this "Why are ye now turned back?" meaning "Why have you not completed your journey?"
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

---

## v. 6: *"They replied, 'A man came up to meet us and said, "Go back to the king who sent you and tell him that this is what the LORD says: Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are sending these men to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore you will not get up from the bed on which you are lying. You will surely die."'"*

The messengers did not name Elijah, calling him simply "a man" (*ish*). The Pulpit Commentary suggests it is unlikely they didn't recognize Elijah — he was too prominent. They may have withheld his name out of goodwill toward Elijah or fear for their own safety (as Obadiah had feared, 1 Kings 18:8–14).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

Guzik notes that "this official delegation from the king would certainly not have turned back from their royal assignment just because some anonymous wayfarer asked them to. There must have been an irresistible quality to Elijah's personality, a forceful spiritual presence, that compelled them to obey."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/

---

## vv. 7–8: *"The king asked them, 'What sort of man came up to meet you and spoke these words to you?' 'He was a hairy man,' they answered, 'with a leather belt around his waist.' 'It was Elijah the Tishbite,' said the king."*

**"A hairy man":** Literally "a lord of hair" (*ba'al se'ar*). Two interpretations exist: (1) he had long, rough, unkempt hair and beard (so the LXX: ἀνὴρ δασύς, "a shaggy man"), or (2) he wore a shaggy garment of untanned animal skin with the hair outward, clinched with a leather belt. The Pulpit Commentary favors the garment interpretation, noting this became associated with prophets generally (Zechariah 13:4) and was worn by John the Baptist (Matthew 3:4). Such rough clothing would only be worn by the very poor and by ascetics — perhaps as a sign of contempt for earthly things, as penitence for Israel's sins, or to "chastise and subdue the flesh."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

Guzik notes the John the Baptist connection: "When the priests and Levites saw him they asked, 'Are you Elijah?' (John 1:19–21)."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/

**Ahaziah's recognition:** The king had no doubt — only Elijah would have the boldness to prophesy the king's death while wearing such a costume. Elijah was Ahaziah's "enemy" as he had been Ahab's "enemy" (1 Kings 21:20). The Pulpit Commentary speculates Ahaziah may have long wanted to arrest Elijah and now saw his opportunity.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

---

## vv. 9–10: *"Then King Ahaziah sent to Elijah a captain with his company of fifty men. So the captain went up to Elijah, who was sitting on top of a hill, and said to him, 'Man of God, the king declares, "Come down!"' Elijah answered the captain, 'If I am a man of God, may fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men.' And fire came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty men."*

**The captain and his fifty:** "Captains of fifties" were first instituted by Jethro's advice (Exodus 18:21–25) and formed part of Israel's military organization. Sending fifty men to arrest one prophet was a show of force — a challenge to see whether Ahaziah or the God Elijah represented was stronger.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

**"Man of God":** The Pulpit Commentary thinks this was spoken respectfully, not ironically. The captain knew Elijah's miraculous reputation and hoped a respectful tone might spare him the prophet's anger. Yet calling Elijah "Man of God" while obeying an ungodly command admitted Elijah's righteousness even while acting against him.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/

**The fire:** Guzik emphasizes that Elijah could not himself bring down fire — only God could. Elijah essentially said: "You say I am a man of God even though you are not acting like it. Let's let God decide by fire." God answered, demonstrating that the insult was not against Elijah personally but against Yahweh. The JFB Commentary concurs: the fire was "not to avenge a personal insult of Elijah, but an insult upon God, in the person of His prophet; and the punishment was inflicted, not by the prophet, but by the direct hand of God." Josephus identifies the fire as lightning.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-kings-1.html (search result excerpt)
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

**A wordplay in Hebrew:** Dr. Constable notes that the captain commanded the "man of God" (*ish ha-elohim*) to "come down." Elijah replied, "If I am a man [*ish*] of God, let fire [*esh*] come down." The wordplay is lost in translation but would have been sharp in Hebrew.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-1.html (search result excerpt)

**The Pulpit Commentary's moral defense:** Elijah was "raised up to vindicate God's honor, to check and punish idolatry." He was "an embodiment of the Law — of absolute, strict, severe justice. The fair face of mercy was not revealed to him." To tax Elijah with cruelty is to involve God in the charge. The judgment was "in accordance with the general tone and tenor of the Law."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

---

## vv. 11–12: *"So the king sent to Elijah another captain with his fifty men. And the captain said to Elijah, 'Man of God, the king declares, "Come down at once!"' Again Elijah replied, 'If I am a man of God, may fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men.' And the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty men."*

The second captain repeated the first captain's error with even greater guilt, since he knew what had happened to the first group. His demand — "Come down at once!" (*quickly*) — was even bolder and more demanding. The Pulpit Commentary speculates that the death of the first captain may have been kept from the king, so he only knew of an unaccountable delay, prompting his impatience.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/

Guzik: "The people and leaders of Israel had gone after pagan gods so long that they could not distinguish between the imaginary, impotent gods of the pagan world and Yahweh, the LORD God of Israel."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/

---

## vv. 13–14: *"So the king sent a third captain with his fifty men. And the third captain went up, fell on his knees before Elijah, and begged him, 'Man of God, may my life and the lives of these fifty servants please be precious in your sight. Behold, fire has come down from heaven and consumed the first two captains of fifty, with all their men. But now may my life be precious in your sight.'"*

The third captain approached in a completely different manner — with humility. He "fell on his knees" and "begged," acknowledging that Elijah truly held his life and the lives of his men at his disposal. He also acknowledged that the fire was divine judgment, not mere chance. The Pulpit Commentary notes he "assumed an attitude, not of command, but of submission."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/

Guzik: "Perhaps the third captain looked at the two blackened spots of scorched earth nearby before he spoke to Elijah."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/

---

## v. 15: *"Then the angel of the LORD said to Elijah, 'Go down with him. Do not be afraid of him.' So Elijah got up and went down with him to the king."*

God's instruction shows it was never that God didn't want Elijah to go to the king — it was that Ahaziah, his captains, and soldiers all acted *as if there were no God in Israel*. When the request was made wisely and humbly, Elijah went. Guzik notes possible reasons Ahaziah wanted to arrest Elijah: to compel him to reverse the word of doom, to show rage against the prophet, or to silence Elijah to discourage future prophets from boldness.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/

JFB calls Elijah's compliance "a marvelous instance of faith and obedience. Though he well knew how obnoxious his presence was to the king, yet on receiving God's command, he goes unhesitatingly."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-kings-1.html (search result excerpt)

---

## v. 16: *"And Elijah said to King Ahaziah, 'This is what the LORD says: Is there really no God in Israel for you to inquire of His word? Is that why you have sent messengers to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore you will not get up from the bed on which you are lying. You will surely die.'"*

Elijah, brought into the royal presence likely as a prisoner, "in no way lowered his tone or abated from the severity of his speech." The message from God did not change just because Ahaziah didn't want to hear it the first time. God's determinations are unalterable.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/

The Pulpit Commentary adds that the king was apparently "abashed and confounded" and released the prophet.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

---

## v. 17: *"So Ahaziah died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken. And since he had no son, Jehoram succeeded him in the second year of the reign of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat over Judah."*

Ahaziah died as prophesied — without leaving his bed, and his death was a judgment on his sin. The proof validated Elijah's prophetic office: the prophecy was fulfilled exactly as spoken.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

**"Jehoram succeeded him":** This Jehoram (also spelled Joram) was another son of Ahab, and thus Ahaziah's brother (2 Kings 3:1). Ahaziah had no son, so the throne passed to his brother. The Pulpit Commentary explains the apparent chronological difficulty (the "second year of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat") by suggesting Jehoshaphat associated his son Jehoram in the kingdom in his own seventeenth year (a practice of co-regency attested in Egypt and seen in David's proclamation of Solomon as king). Thus the second year of Judah's Jehoram coincided with the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/

---

## v. 18: *"As for the rest of the acts of Ahaziah, along with his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?"*

The standard closing formula for the kings of Israel. The Pulpit Commentary suggests these "rest of the acts" may have included months of warfare against Mesha of Moab, whose war of independence consisted of a succession of sieges recovering Israelite-held strongholds (Medeba, Ataroth, Nebo, Jahaz, and others). The Moabite Stone's account of these campaigns is "a striking testimony to the contemporary record of historical events by the Palestinian monarchs of the time."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

Gill adds simply: the acts of Ahaziah were recorded "in which were written his father Ahab's also, and his predecessors'."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/1.htm

---

## Denominational / Theological Distinctives

Given the search and fetch constraints, I was unable to access in-depth denominational commentaries from Baptist (Spurgeon, desiringgod.org, gty.org), Reformed (ligonier.org, monergism.com), Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu), or Catholic/Orthodox sources. What follows is noted from the available material:

**The fire-from-heaven judgment:** A key theological debate in this chapter concerns whether Elijah was right to call down fire. The Pulpit Commentary (Anglican-influenced, broadly Protestant) defends Elijah by arguing he was "an embodiment of the Law — of absolute, strict, severe justice" and that the punishment "was not Elijah's work, but His [God's]." This aligns with the traditional Protestant reading that God, not Elijah, executed the judgment.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

Guzik (Enduring Word/Pentecostal-charismatic) emphasizes that "Elijah could not bring down fire from heaven without Divine approval" and frames the issue as letting "God decide by fire" — consistent with a charismatic emphasis on divine power vindicating the prophet.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-1/

**New Testament connection:** Luke 9:54–56 records that James and John wanted to call down fire from heaven on a Samaritan village, referencing Elijah. Jesus rebuked them, saying, "You do not know what manner of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man did not come to destroy men's lives but to save them." The Pulpit Commentary addresses this implicitly by noting Elijah belonged to the dispensation of Law, not the fuller revelation of mercy in Christ. No specific denominational treatment of this contrast was found in the available sources.

**"Angel of the LORD" as Christophany:** Dr. Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary, dispensational) identifies the angel as "perhaps the preincarnate Christ," reflecting a conservative evangelical/dispensational tendency to see Christophanies in Old Testament angelic appearances.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-1.html (search result excerpt)

By contrast, the Pulpit Commentary simply reads "an angel" (following the LXX), reflecting a more restrained Anglican approach.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-1.html

**Beelzebub in the NT:** Precept Austin notes that the NT preserved the name in the form "Beelzebul" — the Jews changed the vowels of pagan gods' names to mock them. "It can be translated as 'Lord of the house,' 'Lord of the flies,' or 'Lord of the dung.'" In Matthew 10:25, 12:24, Mark 3:22, and Luke 11:15, it is a name for Satan, the prince of demons.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-1-commentary

---

*Note: Due to tool limitations, I was unable to retrieve full content from Baptist (Spurgeon, desiringgod.org, gty.org), Reformed (ligonier.org), Lutheran (lcms.org), Methodist/Wesleyan, Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com), Orthodox (oca.org), or modern scholarship sites (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org). These would need to be consulted separately for their specific readings of this chapter.*
